When a person retires from a prestigious professional position — particularly in a university, a religious institution, or a major organization — they normally lose their title. A professor who retires is no longer "Professor So-and-so." A bishop who steps down is no longer "Bishop So-and-so."

But sometimes, a person's service has been so distinguished, so valuable, and so long-standing that the institution decides: this person deserves to keep their title, even after they retire, as a mark of deep respect and honor.

That is exactly what emeritus means. It is an adjective placed alongside a person's title to signal:

"This person has retired from this role, but they have earned the right to keep the title for life as an honor."

Say Dr. Susan Clark has been a professor at Harvard for 40 years. She has done groundbreaking research, mentored hundreds of students, and brought great prestige to the university. When she retires, Harvard may honor her by designating her Professor Emeritus (or Professor Emerita — more on that shortly).

She is no longer actively teaching or drawing a full salary. She no longer has the usual duties of a professor. But she carries the title Professor Emeritus for the rest of her life. On papers she publishes, on conference name tags, in formal introductions — that title stays with her.
It Is an Honor, Not a Guarantee

This is crucial: not every person who retires gets the emeritus title. You cannot simply clock out after a long career and claim it. The title is awarded — usually by a vote, a committee, or an official decision — and it is reserved for those who served with exceptional distinction. It is the institution's way of saying: "You weren't just an employee. You were outstanding, and we want the world to know that, even now that you've stepped down."

Think of it as a lifetime achievement badge attached to your professional title.

While universities are by far the most common setting, emeritus appears in other places too:

  • Academia: Professor Emeritus, Dean Emeritus, President Emeritus (of a university)
  • Religion: Pope Emeritus (when Pope Benedict XVI resigned in 2013, he became Pope Emeritus Benedict XVI)
  • Corporations and nonprofits: Chairman Emeritus, Director Emeritus
  • Government and public institutions: Surgeon General Emeritus, and similar

The word travels with the title wherever distinguished retirement needs to be recognized.
The Gender Forms: Emeritus, Emerita, and Emeriti

Traditionally, this word has three forms depending on gender and number:

  • Emeritus — used for a man (Professor Emeritus)
  • Emerita — used for a woman (Professor Emerita)
  • Emeriti — used for a group of people (The professors emeriti gathered for the ceremony)

In modern usage, many institutions now use emeritus as a gender-neutral default regardless of the person's gender, and emeriti as the gender-neutral plural. You will see both the traditional and modern conventions in the real world, so neither will look wrong to you.
Where the Word Sits in a Title

You will notice that "emeritus" can appear in two positions:

  • After the main title: Professor Emeritus, Director Emeritus — this is the most traditional and most common placement.
  • Before the main title: Emeritus Professor, Emeritus Director — also acceptable, and used in some countries and institutions.

Both mean exactly the same thing. The position of the word does not change the meaning.

This is where people sometimes get confused, so let's be sharp about it:

  • It does not mean the person is still actively working in that role.
  • It does not mean they are simply "senior" or "experienced."
  • It does not automatically come with the same authority, duties, or full compensation of the active role.

The person is retired. The title is honorary. The word is about recognition of past service, not a description of a current, active job.

Beyond the technical definition, "emeritus" carries a tone of reverence and gratitude. When you see it next to someone's name, you are being told: this person gave a great deal to this field or institution, they have stepped back, and we honor them for it. It is one of the more dignified words in the English language — quiet, serious, and full of respect.

If you see...It means...

If you see "Professor Emeritus John Smith" — John Smith is a retired professor who earned the right to keep his title because of his exceptional career.

If you see "Dean Emerita Jane Liu" — Jane Liu is a retired dean, and the feminine form of the word is used.

If you see "the university's emeriti faculty" — you are reading about a group of retired professors who have all been honored with emeritus status.

That is the word, fully and completely. One title. One retirement. One lifetime of honor.
